title: Why We Need Sleep
summary: How sleep helps the brain store memories, helps the body grow and heal, and how screens and daily habits affect a good night's rest.
poll: Getting enough sleep is just as important as doing your homework.

versions.title: Why We Sleep
versions.text:
Each night, you get in bed. You shut your eyes. Soon you are asleep. But your body is not at rest. It is hard at work.

Sleep helps your brain. In the day, you learn new things. At night, your brain sorts them. It keeps the facts you need. This makes your memory strong. Then it is easy to learn the next day.

Sleep helps your body, too. Kids grow most in deep sleep. The body can fix and repair itself. Sore legs feel good by the next day.

Kids need a lot of sleep. Most need 9 to 12 hours a night. With too little sleep, it is hard to think. You may feel grumpy. You may get sick more, too.

A screen can keep you up. A phone gives off bright light. The light tells your brain it is day. Then it is hard to fall asleep. Put all screens away one hour before bed.

Good habits help you sleep well. Go to bed at the same time each night. Keep your room dark and quiet. Run and play in the day. Have a calm routine, like a bath and a book. Then sleep well!

versions.title: Why We Need Sleep
versions.text:
Every night, you climb into bed and close your eyes. Soon you are asleep. It may look like you are doing nothing. But your brain and your body are busy all night long.

Sleep is good for your brain. All day, you see and hear new things. At night, your brain sorts them. It keeps what is important. It lets the rest go. This makes your memory strong. After a good night of sleep, it is easier to learn.

Sleep is good for your body, too. When you sleep deeply, your body makes something that helps you grow. It also works to repair itself. Tired muscles get strong again.

Kids need lots of sleep. Most kids your age need 9 to 12 hours each night. If you do not get enough, it is hard to pay attention in class. You may feel cranky. You may also get sick more often.

A screen can make it hard to sleep. Phones, tablets, and TVs give off bright light. The light tricks your brain. It thinks it is still day! So try to turn off screens an hour before bed.

Some habits help you sleep well. Go to bed at the same time each night. Keep your room dark, quiet, and cool. Run and play during the day. Then follow a calm routine, such as reading a book. Your brain and body will thank you!

versions.title: Sleep: Your Body's Night Shift
versions.text:
Think about the last time you had a great night of sleep. You probably woke up feeling fresh and ready to go. That is no accident. While you sleep, your brain and body do big jobs.

Sleep happens in stages. First comes light sleep. Then you sink into deep sleep. It is hard to wake up then. Later comes dream sleep. Your eyes dart back and forth under your lids. You go through these stages a few times each night.

During sleep, your brain sorts everything you learned that day. It saves the key facts and skills. Then you can use them later. This builds your memory. That is why it helps to sleep well before a test.

Sleep also helps your body. In deep sleep, your body sends out a special chemical. It helps you grow. Your body also works to repair tired muscles and fight germs.

Most kids ages 6 to 12 need 9 to 12 hours of sleep each night. Without enough sleep, it is hard to focus in class. You may feel grumpy. You may get sick more often.

A screen can steal your sleep. The bright light from phones and tablets tells your brain it is still day. Fun games and videos keep your mind wide awake, too. It is best to put screens away an hour before bed.

Healthy habits make sleep easier. Go to bed and wake up at the same time every day. Keep your bedroom dark, quiet, and cool. Be active during the day. Skip tea and cola at night. They keep you awake. Finally, try a calm bedtime routine, such as reading a book.

versions.title: Sleep: Your Body's Night Shift
versions.text:
Think about the last time you enjoyed a really good night of sleep. You probably woke up feeling fresh, cheerful, and ready for the day. That is no accident. While you are sleeping, your brain and body are doing some of their most important work.

Sleep is not the same all night long. It happens in stages. First comes light sleep. A small noise can wake you then. Next you sink into deep sleep. Your breathing slows, and it is hard to wake up. Later comes dream sleep, when your eyes dart back and forth under your eyelids. You pass through these stages several times each night.

While you sleep, your brain sorts through everything you learned that day. It saves the important facts and skills. Then you can use them later. This process builds your memory. That is one reason it is wise to sleep well before a big test.

Sleep helps your body, too. During deep sleep, your body releases a special chemical that helps you grow taller. Your body also works to repair tired muscles and to fight off germs.

Most children between the ages of 6 and 12 need 9 to 12 hours of sleep each night. Without enough sleep, it is hard to focus in class. You may feel grumpy. You may catch colds more often.

A screen can steal your sleep. Phones, tablets, and computers give off bright light that tells your brain it is still daytime. Exciting games and videos also keep your mind wide awake. For these reasons, it is best to put screens away about an hour before bedtime.

Healthy habits make sleep much easier. Try to go to bed and wake up at the same time every day, even on weekends. Keep your bedroom dark, quiet, and cool. Be active and play outside during the day. Avoid tea, coffee, and cola in the evening. They contain caffeine, which keeps you awake. Finally, create a calm bedtime routine, such as brushing your teeth and reading a book.

versions.title: The Hidden Work of Sleep
versions.text:
When you finally fall asleep at night, it might seem as if your day has ended. In fact, a whole new kind of work is just beginning. While you rest, your brain and body are busy. Their jobs keep you healthy, help you grow, and prepare you to learn.

Sleep is not one long, steady state. Instead, it moves through stages that repeat in a cycle. You start in light sleep. You can be woken easily then. Next you drift into deep sleep, when your heart rate and breathing slow down. After that comes dream sleep, which scientists call REM sleep, short for "rapid eye movement." Each cycle lasts about an hour and a half. It repeats several times every night.

One of the most important jobs of sleep is building memory. During the day, your brain collects huge amounts of information. At night, it replays and sorts that information. It keeps what matters and stores it so you can find it later. Students who sleep well usually find it easier to concentrate and remember their lessons.

Sleep also helps your body grow and heal. In deep sleep, a gland in your brain releases growth hormone. This chemical messenger helps bones and muscles grow. Your body also repairs tissues and strengthens its defenses against germs.

Doctors say that most children aged 6 to 12 need 9 to 12 hours of sleep each night. Without enough rest, children often feel cranky, have trouble paying attention, and get sick more easily.

When it gets dark in the evening, your brain makes a hormone called melatonin that makes you feel sleepy. Bright light from screens can slow this process down. It tricks your brain into thinking it is still daytime. That is why experts suggest turning off phones and tablets about an hour before bed.

Good sleep habits make a big difference. Keep the same bedtime every night. Make your room dark, quiet, and cool. Stay active during the day. In the evening, avoid tea, coffee, and soft drinks, which contain caffeine. A relaxing routine, such as reading a book, tells your body it is time to rest.

Next you descend into deep sleep, when your heart rate and breathing gradually slow. Finally comes dream sleep, which scientists call REM sleep, short for "rapid eye movement," because your eyes flick back and forth beneath your eyelids. Each cycle lasts roughly an hour and a half, and it repeats several times throughout the night.

Sleep also supports physical growth and healing. During deep sleep, a small gland at the base of your brain releases growth hormone, a chemical messenger that helps bones and muscles develop. Meanwhile, your body repairs damaged tissues and strengthens its natural defenses against infection.

Bright light from screens can delay the release of melatonin and convince your brain that it is still daytime. Furthermore, exciting games and videos keep your mind alert when it should be winding down. For these reasons, experts recommend switching off phones and tablets about an hour before bed.

In the evening, avoid tea, coffee, and soft drinks, which contain caffeine. Finally, a relaxing routine, such as reading a book, signals to your body that it is time to rest.

versions.title: Sleep: The Brain's Essential Night Shift
versions.text:
When you finally drift off at night, it might appear that your day has come to a close. In reality, an entirely different kind of activity is just beginning. While you rest, your brain and body carry out a remarkable series of tasks that preserve your health, encourage physical growth, and prepare you to absorb new information the following day.

Sleep is not a single, uniform condition but a sequence of distinct stages that repeat in a predictable pattern. You begin in light sleep, when even a quiet sound can disturb you. Then you descend into deep sleep, when your heart rate, breathing, and body temperature gradually decline. Eventually you enter REM sleep, named for the "rapid eye movement" that occurs beneath your closed eyelids. This is when most vivid dreaming takes place. Each complete cycle lasts approximately an hour and a half, and it repeats several times before morning.

One of the most valuable functions of sleep is to consolidate memory, which means strengthening new memories and moving them into long-term storage. During the day, your brain collects an enormous quantity of information. At night it replays and reorganizes that material, preserving what is significant and discarding what is not. Researchers have also found evidence that the sleeping brain clears away chemical waste that builds up during waking hours.

Sleep is equally important for physical development. During deep sleep, the pituitary gland at the base of the brain releases much of the body's growth hormone, a chemical messenger that helps bones and muscles develop. Meanwhile, the body repairs damaged tissues and reinforces its immune defenses against infection.

Medical organizations recommend that children between the ages of 6 and 12 obtain 9 to 12 hours of sleep each night. Repeated sleep deprivation can leave young people irritable, inattentive, and more vulnerable to illness.

These patterns are guided by your circadian rhythm, an internal clock that follows a cycle of roughly twenty-four hours and is set mainly by daylight. As darkness falls, the brain releases melatonin, a hormone that produces drowsiness. Bright light from electronic screens can delay melatonin and confuse this clock, which is why specialists advise switching off devices approximately an hour before bed.

Healthy habits support this natural system. Maintaining a consistent bedtime, keeping the bedroom dark, quiet, and cool, exercising during the day, and avoiding caffeinated drinks such as tea, coffee, and many soft drinks in the evening all help. A calm routine, such as reading, tells the body that rest is approaching.

questions.why: The article says screen light can delay melatonin and trick the brain into thinking it is still daytime.

wrong.A: Growth hormone is released during deep sleep, not because of screens.
wrong.B: The article does not say screens end dream sleep.
wrong.D: Sorting memories happens during sleep; screens make it harder to fall asleep.

questions.stem: Why does the article mention that growth hormone is released during deep sleep?
options: To prove that children should sleep less
To show that sleep helps children's bodies develop
To explain why people dream at night
To show that hormones come from screens
questions.why: Growth hormone helps bones and muscles grow, so it shows sleep is important for a growing body.

wrong.A: The fact supports getting enough sleep, not less.
wrong.C: Dreaming is linked to REM sleep, not growth hormone.
wrong.D: Hormones are made in the body, not by screens.

questions.stem: Yusuf drinks two cups of tea after dinner and then can't fall asleep. What is the most likely reason?
options: The tea has caffeine, which keeps him awake.
The tea makes his bedroom too dark.
The tea makes his sleep cycle much shorter.
The tea makes his brain release melatonin.
questions.why: The article says to avoid tea, coffee, and soft drinks in the evening because they contain caffeine.

wrong.B: Tea cannot change how dark a room is.
wrong.C: The article does not say tea changes the length of a cycle.
wrong.D: Melatonin makes you sleepy, so it would not keep him awake.

questions.stem: How does the author organize most of the article?
options: By telling events in the order of one child's day
By comparing sleep long ago with sleep today
By explaining what sleep does, then giving tips
By listing questions and answers from doctors
questions.why: The article first explains stages, memory, growth, and melatonin, then ends with healthy sleep habits.

wrong.A: The article does not follow one child through a day.
wrong.B: Sleep long ago is not discussed.

MID.prompt: Explain how sleep helps a student do well in school. Use at least two details from the article to support your answer.
checklist: I gave a clear answer to the question.
I supported my answer with at least two details from the article.
I explained how each detail connects to learning at school.

keyWords.definition: to make something stronger and more lasting by joining or organizing it
keyWords.example: Reviewing your notes each evening helps consolidate what you learned.

keyWords.definition: describing the body's natural daily cycle of about 24 hours
keyWords.example: Flying to a faraway country can upset your circadian clock.

keyWords.definition: a hormone the brain releases in darkness that makes a person feel sleepy
keyWords.example: Dim lights in the evening allow the brain to release melatonin.

keyWords.definition: a chemical messenger made in the body that controls processes such as growth
keyWords.example: Doctors measured the hormone to understand why the boy was growing slowly.

keyWords.definition: the state of not having enough of something that you need
keyWords.example: Water deprivation is a serious danger for travelers in the desert.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Sleep is wasted time that students should reduce.
Electronic screens are the main cause of all illness.
REM sleep matters more than every other stage.
Sleep is active work that supports learning and growth.
questions.why: The article argues that sleep consolidates memory, supports growth and health, and should be protected with habits.

wrong.A: The article argues the opposite: sleep is not wasted time.
wrong.B: Screens are discussed only as a cause of delayed sleep.
wrong.C: The article describes all stages and does not rank REM above the others.

questions.stem: According to the article, what sets the circadian rhythm?
options: Mainly exposure to daylight
Mainly the food a person eats
Mainly the number of dreams
Mainly the growth hormone level
questions.why: The article says the internal clock is synchronized primarily by daylight.

wrong.B: Food is not mentioned as what sets the clock.
wrong.C: Dreams happen in REM sleep but do not set the clock.
wrong.D: Growth hormone is released in deep sleep; it does not set the clock.

questions.stem: Which gland releases growth hormone during deep sleep?
options: The thyroid gland in the neck
The pituitary gland in the brain
The sweat glands in the skin
The salivary glands in the mouth
questions.why: The article states that the pituitary gland at the base of the brain releases growth hormone.

wrong.A: The thyroid is not mentioned in the article.
wrong.C: Sweat glands are not connected to growth hormone in the article.

questions.stem: The article says sleep helps "consolidate memory." Which phrase best explains this term?
options: throwing away facts that are not needed
clearing chemical waste from the brain
moving new memories into long-term storage
repeating several times every single night
questions.why: Consolidating memory means strengthening new memories and moving them into long-term storage.

wrong.A: Discarding is part of sorting, but it does not explain strengthening memories.
wrong.B: Clearing waste is a separate finding about the sleeping brain.
wrong.D: This phrase describes the sleep cycle, not memory.

questions.stem: According to the article, why do specialists advise switching off devices before bedtime?
options: Screen light can postpone melatonin and disrupt the body clock.
Devices use energy that the body needs for growth.
Screens erase memories formed during the school day.
Devices lower body temperature during deep sleep.
questions.why: The article links intense screen light to delayed melatonin and a disrupted circadian clock.

wrong.B: The article does not say devices take the body's energy.
wrong.C: Screens are not said to erase memories.
wrong.D: Body temperature drops naturally in deep sleep; screens are not the cause.

questions.stem: Based on the article, why might a student who stays up late studying remember less than one who sleeps?
options: Studying at night prevents any growth hormone from being made.
Losing sleep reduces the time the brain has to consolidate learning.
Late studying causes the circadian rhythm to stop working.
The student will dream about the lesson and confuse the facts.
questions.why: Since memory is consolidated during sleep, cutting sleep short limits that process.

wrong.A: The article does not say late studying stops all growth hormone.
wrong.C: The article says light can disrupt the clock, not make it stop.
wrong.D: The article does not say dreams confuse facts.

questions.stem: What can the reader infer from the finding that the sleeping brain clears away waste?
options: The brain stops all activity during sleep.
Waste in the brain is caused only by screens.
Only adults need sleep to clear brain waste.
Sleep may help the mind feel clear and alert.
questions.why: The article suggests this finding may explain why too little sleep leaves people mentally sluggish.

wrong.A: Clearing waste is activity, so the brain does not stop working.
wrong.B: The waste builds up during waking hours, not because of screens.
wrong.C: The article does not limit this finding to adults.

questions.stem: Why does the author end the article with a list of healthy habits?
options: To show readers practical ways to protect their sleep
To prove that tea and coffee are unhealthy drinks
To compare sleep habits in different countries
To describe the author's own bedtime experience
questions.why: After explaining why sleep matters, the author gives practical steps readers can take.

wrong.B: Caffeine is mentioned only as something to avoid in the evening.
wrong.C: The article does not compare countries.
wrong.D: The author does not describe personal experience.

HIGH.prompt: Some students believe that staying up late to study is better than sleeping. Do you agree or disagree? Support your position with evidence from the article.
checklist: I supported it with at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
I explained how my evidence supports my position.
